title: Threat Hunting with Intelligence
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Threat Hunting with Intelligence.
Apply threat hunting with intelligence to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers threat hunting with intelligence in the Threat Intelligence and Adversary Behavior track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Treat indicators as time-sensitive and potentially noisy; an indicator alone does not prove compromise. The specific focus here is threat hunting with intelligence; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Threat Hunting with Intelligence focuses on turning intelligence into hunting questions; searching historical events; behavior-based hunting. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
# Documentation-only TEST-NET indicator; not a real threat IOC.
known_indicator = "203.0.113.10"
sample_events = ["192.0.2.15", "203.0.113.10", "198.51.100.8"]
matched = [address for address in sample_events if address == known_indicator]
print("synthetic matches:", len(matched))
print("evidence required before incident declaration: yes")
content_blocks.expected_output:
synthetic matches: 1
evidence required before incident declaration: yes
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Threat intelligence adds value when observations are contextualized, assessed for confidence and relevance, and connected to a defensive decision. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.text: Recap: Threat Hunting with Intelligence focuses on turning intelligence into hunting questions; searching historical events; behavior-based hunting. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Threat Hunting with Intelligence. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Turning Intelligence into Hunting Questions; Searching Historical Events; Behavior-Based Hunting), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Threat Hunting with Intelligence is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.

sources.title: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Matrix
sources.notes: ATT&CK catalogs tactics and techniques from observed adversary behavior; it is not a deterministic attack timeline or proof that any one intrusion follows every stage.

sources.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) Version 4.0
sources.publisher: Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST)
sources.notes: CVSS is a vulnerability-severity framework, not a complete organizational risk score or a replacement for threat context and business impact.
